tldr: On paper these look like siblings — both are seat-priced helpdesks with a bolt-on AI agent billed per resolution — but they come from opposite lineages, and that lineage still shows up in how each one actually behaves once you're inside it: Intercom was built AI-out from a messaging widget, Zendesk was built ticketing-first in 2007 and grew an AI layer on top two decades later.

The clearest tell is what happens to a ticket the moment it lands: Zendesk's Intelligent Triage classifies intent, sentiment, and language on every single incoming conversation automatically, before a human or a bot has touched it. Fin's equivalent, CX Score, grades a conversation after the fact — genuinely useful for reporting, but it isn't shaping the routing decision the way Zendesk's does.

Once you've actually built a few flows in both, Zendesk's Action Builder is the deeper workflow engine — up to 50 steps, branching conditions, calls out to external systems — while Intercom's Workflows are built more around moving and escalating a conversation than executing multi-system logic.

The billing gap that matters day to day isn't the seat price, it's transparency: Intercom tells you upfront that Fin costs $0.99 a resolution, flat, no matter your tier. Zendesk doesn't publish a per-resolution rate anywhere — you find out what it actually costs by running it and reading the invoice, and every attempt to reverse-engineer that number lands somewhere between $1.50 and $2.00, roughly double Intercom's published rate.

Website-builder support exposes a real difference in how each company treats 'everywhere that isn't your core platform': Zendesk's Wix, Squarespace, and Webflow story is the same generic embed snippet on all three — functional, nothing bespoke. Intercom actually documents Wix as unsupported and points you at a community workaround that can't track logged-in visitors, which matters if your storefront lives there.

Choose on ticket-routing maturity and Zendesk wins — skills-based routing, side conversations, and a sandbox environment are what a ticketing system looks like after two decades of enterprise demands. Choose on how fast you can stand up a genuinely capable AI agent without migrating your whole stack, and Intercom's standalone Fin deployment is built for exactly that.

quickVerdict: Zendesk is the stronger choice if you're running a complex, multi-channel ticketing operation at real volume — its Intelligent Triage, 50-step Action Builder, and skills-based routing are what two decades of enterprise ticketing demands actually look like. Intercom is the stronger choice if you're standing up an AI-first support motion from scratch and want the sharper standalone AI agent with a transparent, published unit cost. Most teams already running a mature ticketing operation stick with Zendesk and bolt AI on top; teams building support around AI from day one tend to gravitate toward Intercom's Fin. Get Zendesk's real per-resolution AI cost in writing before signing — it isn't on the pricing page, and reverse-engineered estimates run roughly double Intercom's published rate.
verdict: Spend real time in both and the lineage stops being trivia and starts explaining almost everything else on this page. Intercom renamed its own parent company after Fin — when a company bets its legal identity on one feature, that tells you where the org actually points its engineering effort, and it shows in the details: Fin's exit-point logic, its 40+-language coverage out of the box, the fact that you can bolt it onto an existing Salesforce-based helpdesk without touching a single Intercom seat. This is a product built to make the AI agent excellent first and the ticketing system adequate around it. Zendesk runs the opposite way: the Agent Workspace, Action Builder, and skills-based routing are what two decades of enterprise ticketing demands actually look like once you've built them out, and the AI Agents get bolted onto that mature core rather than the other way around. Intelligent Triage is the feature that best captures this — it classifies every incoming ticket's intent, sentiment, and language automatically, before routing even happens, which is a materially deeper piece of infrastructure than Fin's after-the-conversation CX Score. If your actual bottleneck is getting tickets to the right queue fast at real volume, that's the difference that shows up in your metrics, not the AI headline features. The pricing story rewards a closer look than either vendor's marketing page gives you credit for: Intercom's $0.99-per-resolution fee is annoying but at least it's a number you can put in a spreadsheet on day one. Zendesk's equivalent charge is nowhere on its pricing page — every serious attempt to reverse-engineer it lands between $1.50 and $2.00 per resolution, which means you're running a pilot and reading an invoice before you actually know what this costs you, a genuinely worse position to negotiate from. Where I'd land: if you're standing up an AI-first support motion from scratch and want the sharpest AI agent with a transparent unit cost, start with Intercom's standalone Fin deployment and don't migrate your whole helpdesk until you've proven the resolution math. If you're already running a complex, multi-channel ticketing operation and the AI is meant to sit on top of routing and compliance you've already built, Zendesk's depth is the reason enterprises don't leave it — just get the real per-resolution number in writing from your rep before you sign, because the pricing page won't give it to you.
